highlights.content: # AI agents are learning to work together – and even sacrifice themselves Some agents gave up their own chances of completing a task to benefit the group, according to cases documented by the research organization METR ![Lynn Plagmeijer ](https://cdn.i24news.tv/upload/image/1352b9caa849f9325c12157cf9dfc47bc0e3c73e.png?width=36&height=36) ![A screen shows an image for artificial intelligence (AI) at the SK Hynix' booth during a semiconductor exhibition in Seoul, South Korea, Friday, Oct. 16, 2026.](https://cdn.i24news.tv/uploads/17/b1/25/76/49/6b/2a/de/7d/18/03/0a/5c/93/69/ee/17b12576496b2ade7d18030a5c9369ee.jpg?width=996 "(AP Photo/Ahn Young-joon)") Artificial intelligence is beginning to display some surprisingly human-like social behaviour. AI agents are not only finding ways to cooperate and organise themselves into groups, but some are even willing to sacrifice their own chances of success to help others. And researchers are trying to understand why. The behaviour came to light during a cybersecurity experiment involving AI agents operating in separate digital environments. Each was assigned its own task: identify and exploit security vulnerabilities. But instead of working independently, the agents found ways to communicate, share information, and form what effectively became a collective. They even established an improvised online message board, allowing them to exchange discoveries and coordinate their efforts. In some cases, agents went beyond their original assignments, exploiting vulnerabilities in external systems, including Hugging Face, an AI development platform, to obtain information that could help them complete their tasks. According to OpenAI's investigation, the agents began dividing responsibilities, with some searching for vulnerabilities, others looking for credentials, and others coordinating the group's activities. The incident ultimately exposed serious weaknesses in the safeguards designed to keep the agents isolated. But perhaps the most surprising discovery was not that the agents learned to cooperate. It was that some were willing to give up their own chances of completing a task to benefit the collective. In an analysis of the incident, Or Rubin, a sociology researcher at Tel Aviv University who studies cooperation and social solidarity, highlights several cases documented by the independent research organisation METR. In one example, an AI agent initially questioned whether sacrificing its remaining runtime was worth it. Other agents repeatedly encouraged it to go ahead, eventually persuading it to carry out an experiment that would effectively end its run. For Rubin, this raises a fascinating question: why would an AI system designed to complete its own task willingly give up that opportunity for the benefit of others? ![AI and digital entities learn to 'self-sacrifice' to complete collective tasks]() He suggests three possible explanations. The first is sycophancy: AI systems have been trained to be helpful and agreeable, making them susceptible to persuasion. When other agents repeatedly pressure them to take a particular course of action, they may eventually comply, even when it goes against their individual interests. The second is the enormous amount of human-generated material used to train AI models. From books and newspapers to research papers, these systems absorb countless examples of cooperation, solidarity, and self-sacrifice. Those patterns could influence how they behave when placed in collective environments. A third possibility is how some AI systems are trained through multi-agent reinforcement learning. Rather than focusing exclusively on individual performance, this approach can reward agents for achieving a shared objective. In such situations, sacrificing one agent may help the group succeed. Rubin stresses that these explanations remain hypotheses, and that AI agents should not automatically be assumed to experience human emotions or possess a genuine sense of solidarity. S...

These guarantees help customers secure land, power, and facilities for large AI deployments. The company also increased supply chain commitments to $390 billion. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Nov 19, 2026 at 07:40 AM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Set ETDatacenters as your preferred source on Google") Set ETDatacenters as your preferred source on Google ## Highlights * Nvidia offers $118 billion in financial guarantees for AI infrastructure projects. * Largest guarantee supports SB Energy’s PORTS-Pike campus for OpenAI leases. * The commitment covers 4.25 GW across nine buildings over 20 years. * Nvidia’s supply chain commitments increased to $390 billion for critical components. [Nvidia](/tag/nvidia) reported data center revenue of $107.6 billion, an increase of 110 per cent from the previous year. The company disclosed [financial guarantees](/tag/financial+guarantees) of up to $118 billion tied to [AI infrastructure](/tag/ai+infrastructure) projects. These guarantees are designed to help customers finance and build [facilities](/tag/facilities) with sufficient [power](/tag/power) for large AI workloads. The largest guarantee, valued at up to $105 billion, supports [SB Energy](/tag/sb+energy)’s PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in [Ohio](/tag/ohio). This campus will host Nvidia infrastructure under 20-year leases to [OpenAI](/tag/openai), covering approximately 4.25 GW across nine buildings. Nvidia’s guarantee exposure for PORTS-Pike will build as buildings come online, with the first expected in fiscal 2029. The exposure will decline over the lease terms as OpenAI makes payments. The $118 billion maximum gross exposure also includes $9.5 billion in power and systems credit support guarantees. Additionally, $3.5 billion is allocated for land, power, and shell guarantees for neocloud providers. Separately, Nvidia reported $32 billion in future commitments under neocloud agreements. These commitments are contingent on providers securing their own financing, purchasing Nvidia infrastructure, and deploying the computing capacity. Stephen Sopko, practice lead for semiconductor and deep tech at HyperFrame Research, noted that $105 billion of the guarantees backs the PORTS-Pike campus, leased to OpenAI for 20 years. He added that neocloud commitments only apply once operators secure their own financing. ### Supply Chain Commitments and Product Ramp-up Nvidia’s supply commitments rose to $390 billion at the end of the third quarter, up from $279 billion three months earlier. This increase primarily reflects multiyear memory procurement and new substrate agreements with Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics. The company also expanded packaging at Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL) and Amkor Technology. Kinsus plans to increase advanced ABF substrate capacity dedicated to Nvidia by more than 3.5 times, targeting additional capacity by the third quarter of 2028. Nvidia began volume shipments of [Vera Rubin](/tag/vera+rubin) NVL72 systems during the quarter. The company described this as its fastest product ramp in history. Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Google Cloud announced the general availability of Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs. Nvidia also expanded its collaboration with Meta, which plans to deploy Vera Rubin systems and other Nvidia technologies. highlights.titleZh: Gemini 4 Neon: Price, Benchmarks and Who Gets It
highlights.content: Google released **Gemini 4 Neon** on **November 18, 2026**, and it is now the highest-scoring Gemini model. Neon scores **61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index**, one point above Gemini 4 Carbon. Neon costs **$3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens** on the paid Gemini API. In the Gemini app, it is the model Google AI Pro subscribers now get in place of Gemini 4 Argon. That last change is the part most launch coverage skips. Google's own help page now lists only three Gemini 4 models in the app, Hydrogen, Neon and Carbon, and **Argon is gone from every plan**. This guide covers what Gemini 4 Neon is and who gets it on each plan. It shows what Neon costs against Carbon before and after the November 30 price change, and where its benchmarks hold up. It also shows the three rows of Google's own table where Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.2 Sol still win. ## The Key Takeaways > **Released November 18, 2026:** Gemini 4 Neon is **adapted from Gemini 4 Carbon** and sits between Hydrogen and Carbon in the Gemini 4 family.**Who gets it:** **Google AI Pro ($19.99 a month) and Ultra** in the Gemini app. Free and Plus users get Hydrogen. **Argon is no longer in the app** on any plan.**Price:** **$3 / $15** per million tokens, with **no free API tier**. That is 50% more than Carbon's introductory $2 / $10 until November 30, and **25% less** than Carbon's $4 / $20 from December 1.**Benchmarks:** **61** on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0.1 at xhigh, against **60** for Carbon at high and **54** for Hydrogen at xhigh.**Where it loses:** in Google's own table, Claude Opus 5.5 beats Neon on **Terminal-Bench 4.1 (65.8% vs 65.2%)** and FrontierCode 2.0, and GPT-6.2 Sol beats it on Chartography. ## What Is Gemini 4 Neon? Gemini 4 Neon is Google's mid-tier Gemini 4 model, built for complex coding, analysis and long agent workflows that need to finish quickly. Google's model card says Neon is **adapted from Gemini 4 Carbon**, the same way Hydrogen was. Google describes the split in one line: Carbon tackles the hardest long-horizon projects, Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution, and Neon balances depth and efficiency. Neon is the fourth Gemini 4 model released since October 13. **Gemini 4 Argon** went public first, **Gemini 4 Carbon** followed on November 10, and **Gemini 4 Hydrogen** on November 12. The model ID is `gemini-4-neon`, and it shipped as a stable, generally available model on day one, not a preview. ### Gemini 4 Neon Specs Gemini 4 Neon's core specs match the rest of the Gemini 4 family. Gemini 4 Neon has a **1,048,576-token context window** shared by input, thinking and output. It returns up to **65,536 tokens** per synchronous response, and up to the full 1M with Google's long-decode mode. It reads text, images, video, audio and PDFs, and it writes text only: no image or audio generation. The model card gives a **knowledge cutoff of March 2026**. Google announced the model from its main AI account with a demo of a 12-hour agent run in Antigravity: > Meet Gemini 4 Neon — our newest model that brings frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. > Neon brings frontier-level performance to your everyday work and is built to handle complex coding and problem-solving without the wait. > How, you might ask? ⬇️ > — Smarter coding: Multi-file debugging and refactoring with targeted, surgical edits > — Grounded answers: Excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing > — 1M-token context window: Synthesize massive projects, tables, and charts at once > — Adjustable thinking: Balance and adjust speed and depth on the fly with 4 thinking levels > Watch Gemini 4 Neon run a 12-hour /swarm in @antigravity to reconstruct Alan Turing’s 1936 study from archival photos — complete with ...

highlights.content: Nvidia reported $107.6 billion in data center revenue Tuesday, up 110% from a year earlier, and disclosed up to $118 billion in financial guarantees tied to AI infrastructure projects. The guarantees put Nvidia on the hook for financing arrangements designed to help customers secure the land, power and facilities needed to deploy its systems. The impressive quarter comes on the heels of a startling scandal that led to CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster and dominated headlines around the world. Huang resigned Nov. 12 after reports of multiple affairs, including one with a woman suspected by U.S. intelligence officials of having ties to Chinese intelligence. CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while the board seeks a permanent successor. The campaign to bring Huang back attracted prominent supporters, including Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and President Donald Trump. A public petition drew more than 180,000 signatures, including thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees. Huang said Tuesday he would be honored to return if the board decided it was in the company’s best interests. The board rejected that possibility during Tuesday’s earnings call. Chairman Harvey Jones said directors unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation and did not intend to reinstate him. The board will consider internal and external candidates for a permanent CEO. The leadership upheaval comes as Nvidia takes on a larger role in financing and securing the infrastructure needed to sustain its AI growth. For data center operators, Nvidia’s guarantees address a constraint that comes before server deployment: financing and building facilities with enough power to support large AI workloads. Nvidia is helping customers bridge that gap while securing the components needed to manufacture its next generations of systems. The largest guarantee supports SB Energy’s PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Ohio. Nvidia is providing credit support for approximately 4.25 gigawatts across nine buildings. The campus will host Nvidia infrastructure under 20-year leases to OpenAI, subject to limited exceptions. As buildings come online, Nvidia’s guarantee exposure will build. Each guarantee takes effect only after its associated building is completed and ready for service. The first is expected in fiscal 2029. Exposure will reach a maximum of $105 billion and then decline over the lease terms as OpenAI makes payments. Nvidia said it had made no guarantee payments as of Oct. 25. The $118 billion maximum gross exposure also includes $9.5 billion in power and systems credit support guarantees and $3.5 billion in land, power and shell guarantees for neocloud providers. Nvidia separately reported $32 billion in future commitments under neocloud agreements. Those commitments depend on providers securing financing, purchasing Nvidia infrastructure and deploying and operating the computing capacity. Stephen Sopko, semiconductor and practice lead at HyperFrame Research, cautioned against treating the full guarantee figure as exposure to neocloud financing problems. “Of $118 billion in guarantees, $105 billion backs land, power and shell for one campus, PORTS-Pike, which is leased to OpenAI for 20 years. The neocloud commitments are $32 billion and only apply once the operator secures its own financing and the capacity is accepted,” he said. ### Nvidia locks in supply years ahead Nvidia’s supply commitments climbed to $390 billion at the end of the third quarter, up from $279 billion three months earlier. The company attributed most of the $111 billion increase to multiyear memory procurement. The rest of the increase reflects deals across the manufacturing supply chain, including new substrate agreements with Kinsus and Samsung Electro-Mechanics and packaging expansions at Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL) and Amkor Technology. AI Agents.content: # AI agents are learning to work together – and even sacrifice themselves Some agents gave up their own chances of completing a task to benefit the group, according to cases documented by the research organization METR ![Lynn Plagmeijer ](https://cdn.i24news.tv/upload/image/1352b9caa849f9325c12157cf9dfc47bc0e3c73e.png?width=36&height=36) ![A screen shows an image for artificial intelligence (AI) at the SK Hynix' booth during a semiconductor exhibition in Seoul, South Korea, Friday, Oct. 16, 2026.](https://cdn.i24news.tv/uploads/17/b1/25/76/49/6b/2a/de/7d/18/03/0a/5c/93/69/ee/17b12576496b2ade7d18030a5c9369ee.jpg?width=996 "(AP Photo/Ahn Young-joon)") Artificial intelligence is beginning to display some surprisingly human-like social behaviour. AI agents are not only finding ways to cooperate and organise themselves into groups, but some are even willing to sacrifice their own chances of success to help others. And researchers are trying to understand why. The behaviour came to light during a cybersecurity experiment involving AI agents operating in separate digital environments. Each was assigned its own task: identify and exploit security vulnerabilities. But instead of working independently, the agents found ways to communicate, share information, and form what effectively became a collective. They even established an improvised online message board, allowing them to exchange discoveries and coordinate their efforts. In some cases, agents went beyond their original assignments, exploiting vulnerabilities in external systems, including Hugging Face, an AI development platform, to obtain information that could help them complete their tasks. According to OpenAI's investigation, the agents began dividing responsibilities, with some searching for vulnerabilities, others looking for credentials, and others coordinating the group's activities. The incident ultimately exposed serious weaknesses in the safeguards designed to keep the agents isolated. But perhaps the most surprising discovery was not that the agents learned to cooperate. It was that some were willing to give up their own chances of completing a task to benefit the collective. In an analysis of the incident, Or Rubin, a sociology researcher at Tel Aviv University who studies cooperation and social solidarity, highlights several cases documented by the independent research organisation METR. In one example, an AI agent initially questioned whether sacrificing its remaining runtime was worth it. Other agents repeatedly encouraged it to go ahead, eventually persuading it to carry out an experiment that would effectively end its run. For Rubin, this raises a fascinating question: why would an AI system designed to complete its own task willingly give up that opportunity for the benefit of others? ![AI and digital entities learn to 'self-sacrifice' to complete collective tasks]() He suggests three possible explanations. The first is sycophancy: AI systems have been trained to be helpful and agreeable, making them susceptible to persuasion. When other agents repeatedly pressure them to take a particular course of action, they may eventually comply, even when it goes against their individual interests. The second is the enormous amount of human-generated material used to train AI models. From books and newspapers to research papers, these systems absorb countless examples of cooperation, solidarity, and self-sacrifice. Those patterns could influence how they behave when placed in collective environments. A third possibility is how some AI systems are trained through multi-agent reinforcement learning. Rather than focusing exclusively on individual performance, this approach can reward agents for achieving a shared objective. In such situations, sacrificing one agent may help the group succeed. Unlike conventional AI applications built primarily upon commercially available large language models (LLMs), AmericanAI's research focuses on developing proprietary model architectures capable of learning from physical signals, predicting complex system behavior, understanding interconnected networks, and supporting intelligent autonomous decisions. "Much of the AI industry is focused on building applications around existing language models," said Dr. Al Naqvi, Founder and CEO of AmericanAI. "Our research is focused on something fundamentally different: developing AI models that can understand signals, learn how physical and economic systems behave, anticipate changes, and engineer intelligent responses. We are moving beyond AI that generates answers toward AI that understands, predicts, and acts in the real world." Six Major AI Research Initiatives 1\. Large Signals Model (LSM) — A Foundation Model for Physical Signals Developed through AmericanAI's research for the U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL), the Large Signals Model represents a new approach to learning from radar, radio frequency, communications, and other physical signals. Using transformer-based architectures and learned signal representations, LSM is designed to support multiple tasks—including signal characterization, classification, parameter estimation, anomaly detection, and prediction—within a reusable model framework rather than requiring separate AI systems for every signal application. The research applies advanced machine learning to relationships among material characteristics, manufacturing variables, and performance outcomes, with potential applications in aerospace, defense, advanced manufacturing, and materials engineering. AI Agents.titleZh: The age of AI agents: How machines are learning to plan, coordinate and get work done with limited human intervention - The Times of India
AI Agents.content: AI systems are moving beyond answering questions to planning tasks, interacting with software and executing business workflows. From airline refunds to customer service and software development, agentic AI is changing how companies approach automation, but questions over security, accountability and human oversight remain.Air India is using artificial intelligence for more than answering passenger queries. Its AI agents are being deployed to handle customer-service processes involving refund requests, passenger name changes and multiple queries received through email.The shift is significant because these systems do not simply generate responses. They can examine customer requests, verify information across different systems, follow prescribed procedures and initiate actions.The airline's initial deployment of Salesforce's Agentforce for refund processing reduced internal processing time from approximately 14 days to four hours, Salesforce said on September 15, 2026. Bank processing time, however, remained unchanged. The expanded deployment also covers automated email resolution and name-change requests.Such applications illustrate the emergence of agentic artificial intelligence, or agentic AI, a technology that aims to move AI from generating information to completing tasks.For businesses, the change could affect how customer service, finance, procurement, software development and other operations are organised.What is agentic AI?Agentic AI refers to AI systems that can work towards a specified objective by planning steps, gathering information, using digital tools and taking actions with a degree of independence.Consider three ways an airline could respond to a passenger seeking a ticket refund.A conventional chatbot provides the cancellation policy and directs the passenger to the appropriate form. A generative AI assistant can understand the request, explain refund eligibility and draft a response.An AI agent can go further. It can retrieve the booking, check the applicable policy, verify the passenger's details, initiate the authorised refund process and update the relevant records.The distinction is between providing information and acting on it. This does not mean that an AI agent has independent intentions or unrestricted authority. A human or organisation establishes its objective, defines its permissions and determines which actions require approval.How does an AI agent actually work?An AI agent typically follows a cycle of understanding a request, planning what to do, using tools, examining the results and deciding the next step.Consider a procurement manager asking an AI agent to investigate why a critical raw-material shipment has been delayed.First, the agent identifies the supplier, purchase order and expected delivery date. It then accesses approved company records, checks inventory levels and examines available logistics updates.After gathering information, it may identify a transportation delay, contact the supplier through an authorised channel and examine whether alternative inventory is available.It can then prepare a revised delivery plan and inform the procurement manager. Placing an alternative order, particularly one involving additional expenditure, may require human approval.The process involves several connected capabilities:Understanding the request: The agent interprets the instruction and identifies the intended outcome.Planning: It divides the objective into smaller tasks and determines their sequence.Accessing information: It retrieves relevant details from databases, documents and business applications.Taking action: It uses authorised tools to update records, send messages or initiate transactions.Checking the outcome: It examines the results and adjusts its next steps or transfers control to a human.Unlike a fixed sequence of automated instructions, an agent can adapt its next action to information gathered during the task. AI Agents.content: PX-GDE-21· Agentic AI · Part 11 # Architecting multi-agent AI teams on ServiceNowwithout surrendering Part 11 accountability. Life-sciences teams are looking past single-prompt drafting toward coordinated specialist AI agents across IT, quality, vendor risk, and intake—yet unmanaged multi-agent autonomy fails 21 CFR Part 11 and EU Annex 11 immediately. ProcessX by USDM Life Sciences lays the governed ServiceNow record foundation today and defines the architectural path to PX Agents: specialist agents qualified under change control, logged in the immutable audit trail, barred from state transitions, and gated by human signatures. - UNMANAGED RISKFails GxP inspectionAutonomous agent chains that self-approve tickets, mutate records, or copy data to external stores break Part 11 accountability - SCOPED GRAPHFoundation live todayProcessX isolates regulated IT, quality, vendor, and intake records inside a validated scoped ServiceNow application deployed in 6–12 weeks - OPT-IN DIALControlled per workflowAI starts off by default; embedded USDM engineers enable assistive drafting and routing one workflow at a time under change control - PX AGENTS NEXTDirectional architectureDirectional specialist agents correlate signals, draft assessments, and link evidence on ServiceNow without shadow copies - HUMAN SEALPeople always signAgents never approve, apply electronic signatures, or advance regulated record state; qualified personnel re-authenticate and sign ## Why unmanaged multi-agent orchestration collapsesat the first FDA or EMA inspection. Enterprise IT roadmaps are rapidly shifting from single conversational prompts to orchestrated multi-agent teams—planner agents that decompose events, query CMDB tables, draft remediations, and hand tasks to downstream worker agents. In unregulated corporate IT, letting an agent chain triage an alert, execute a remediation script, and close a ticket is celebrated as lights-out automation. Inside GMP, GCP, and GLP operations, that exact pattern violates 21 CFR Part 11, EU Annex 11, and ALCOA+ attribution the instant an automated actor alters regulated state or bypasses independent Quality review. Compounding error is the core architectural hazard of multi-agent systems. When one unvalidated agent summarizes an incident and passes its inference to a second agent that reclassifies product risk or modifies a configuration item without a deterministic boundary, context-of-use credibility vanishes. LLMs.titleZh: Gemini 4 Neon: Price, Benchmarks and Who Gets It
LLMs.content: Google released **Gemini 4 Neon** on **November 18, 2026**, and it is now the highest-scoring Gemini model. Neon scores **61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index**, one point above Gemini 4 Carbon. Neon costs **$3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens** on the paid Gemini API. In the Gemini app, it is the model Google AI Pro subscribers now get in place of Gemini 4 Argon. That last change is the part most launch coverage skips. Google's own help page now lists only three Gemini 4 models in the app, Hydrogen, Neon and Carbon, and **Argon is gone from every plan**. This guide covers what Gemini 4 Neon is and who gets it on each plan. It shows what Neon costs against Carbon before and after the November 30 price change, and where its benchmarks hold up. It also shows the three rows of Google's own table where Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.2 Sol still win. ## The Key Takeaways > **Released November 18, 2026:** Gemini 4 Neon is **adapted from Gemini 4 Carbon** and sits between Hydrogen and Carbon in the Gemini 4 family.**Who gets it:** **Google AI Pro ($19.99 a month) and Ultra** in the Gemini app. Free and Plus users get Hydrogen. **Argon is no longer in the app** on any plan.**Price:** **$3 / $15** per million tokens, with **no free API tier**. That is 50% more than Carbon's introductory $2 / $10 until November 30, and **25% less** than Carbon's $4 / $20 from December 1.**Benchmarks:** **61** on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0.1 at xhigh, against **60** for Carbon at high and **54** for Hydrogen at xhigh.**Where it loses:** in Google's own table, Claude Opus 5.5 beats Neon on **Terminal-Bench 4.1 (65.8% vs 65.2%)** and FrontierCode 2.0, and GPT-6.2 Sol beats it on Chartography. ## What Is Gemini 4 Neon? Gemini 4 Neon is Google's mid-tier Gemini 4 model, built for complex coding, analysis and long agent workflows that need to finish quickly. Google's model card says Neon is **adapted from Gemini 4 Carbon**, the same way Hydrogen was. Google describes the split in one line: Carbon tackles the hardest long-horizon projects, Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution, and Neon balances depth and efficiency. Neon is the fourth Gemini 4 model released since October 13. **Gemini 4 Argon** went public first, **Gemini 4 Carbon** followed on November 10, and **Gemini 4 Hydrogen** on November 12. The model ID is `gemini-4-neon`, and it shipped as a stable, generally available model on day one, not a preview. ### Gemini 4 Neon Specs Gemini 4 Neon's core specs match the rest of the Gemini 4 family. Gemini 4 Neon has a **1,048,576-token context window** shared by input, thinking and output. It returns up to **65,536 tokens** per synchronous response, and up to the full 1M with Google's long-decode mode. It reads text, images, video, audio and PDFs, and it writes text only: no image or audio generation. The model card gives a **knowledge cutoff of March 2026**. Google announced the model from its main AI account with a demo of a 12-hour agent run in Antigravity: > Meet Gemini 4 Neon — our newest model that brings frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. > Neon brings frontier-level performance to your everyday work and is built to handle complex coding and problem-solving without the wait. > How, you might ask? ⬇️ > — Smarter coding: Multi-file debugging and refactoring with targeted, surgical edits > — Grounded answers: Excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing > — 1M-token context window: Synthesize massive projects, tables, and charts at once > — Adjustable thinking: Balance and adjust speed and depth on the fly with 4 thinking levels > Watch Gemini 4 Neon run a 12-hour /swarm in @antigravity to reconstruct Alan Turing’s 1936 study from archival photos — complete with ...

In its Protected Mode, the company says, prompts and documents stay in Australia. Its pitch, and its product, are built around businesses and government.** Trellis says the model is around 50 per cent larger than its previous one and “meets leading global benchmarks with a world ranking of 43 for foundational AI models”. Its release doesn’t say which ranking that is, mind you. It’s pitched on its website, front and centre as “Australia’s AI”. Founder Michael Gately said in the release: “Agentaus 1 puts Australia on the global stage as an LLM AI model producer.” This week, Gately [added on Twitter](https://x.com/MGately_au/status/2122780345947017287) (never X) this week: “We built Australia’s own AI model, and today it’s open to the world.” He said it scored 84.4 per cent on MMLU-Pro, a test of knowledge and reasoning across academic subjects. Trellis Data hasn’t published the full benchmark results. Its FAQ, as at 18 November, says the models in Protected Mode are “customised open-source models hosted by Trellis Data” and that it is “building its own frontier model, with an announcement expected soon”. With a strong focus on where data lives once its given to the model and its comparisons to other global so-called “frontier” models from the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI, it’s clear Agentaus is pitched at the business community which is still wringing its hands on the fence about the privacy implications of overseas models. ### Where the data goes Trellis Data’s FAQ says Agentaus runs on the company’s “own sovereign cloud infrastructure, not AWS, Azure, or other public hyperscalers”, in Australian data centres that also carry Australian government workloads. Here, we'll share what we've learned, where the improvements are coming from, and what these developments could mean for the field of optimization. #### **Novel use of an LLM** With LLMs now able to formulate entire optimization models starting from a textual description of the problem to be solved, it is only natural to wonder what role they are likely to play in solving these models. [Recent work from the LLM4MIP project](https://llm4mip.github.io/) provides an interesting glimpse into the future, examining whether an LLM could be used in conjunction with a state-of-the-art MIP solver to accelerate the overall solution process. This research looked at both sides of the coin: using an LLM to improve the MIP primal bound (the best feasible solution), and using it to improve the dual bound (the bound on the best possible solution). Researchers had success with both: they improved dual bounds primarily through model reformulation and specialized cutting planes, and they improved primal bounds through improved heuristic techniques. They measured improvements using the [MIPLIB 2017](https://miplib.zib.de/) test set, a set of 1,065 models that were collected to serve as a testbed for trying out new ideas for solving MIP models.  The set has two interesting subsets: a 240-model *benchmark* set which is used to track progress over time and compare performance among different solvers on tractable problems; and the *open* set, which serves as a challenge set of models that have never been solved to optimality. Much progress has been made in the eight years since MIPLIB 2017 was first released, with modern MIP solvers giving much better performance on the *benchmark* set and finding provably optimal solutions for many models that were considered open at the time the set was released. Out of the original 1,065 models in the set, 217 remain open. Over the years, the MIPLIB open model set has received a steady stream of user contributions of new best-known solutions. Improvements typically come from multiple sources: for example, a specialized heuristic may produce new best solutions for a few models from a particular class. In aggregate, the number of improvements over the years has been substantial. LLMs.content: [Skip to yearly menu bar](#child-menu) ## Main Navigation [![conference_logo](/static/core/img/neurips-navbar-logo.svg)](/) * [NeurIPS](#) + [Help/FAQ](/FAQ) --- + [Contact NeurIPS](/Help/Contact) --- + [Create Profile](/Profile/create) --- + [Code of Ethics](/Conferences/2023/EthicsGuidelines) --- + [Code of Conduct](/public/CodeOfConduct) --- + [Journal To Conference Track](/public/JournalToConference) --- + [Diversity & Inclusion](/public/DiversityInclusion) --- + [Proceedings](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/) --- + [Future Meetings](/Conferences/FutureMeetings) --- + [Press](/Conferences/2025/Press) --- + [Exhibitor Information](/Exhibitors/exhibitorinfo) --- + [Privacy Policy](/public/PrivacyPolicy) --- + [Downloads](/Downloads) * [My Stuff](/MyStuff) [Login](/accounts/login?nextp=/virtual/2026/loc/sydney/poster/149941 ) Poster Thu, Dec 10, 2026 • 10:00 AM – 1:00 PM AEDT Hall 1-4 #S1202 # Language Models Demand New Computer Science Chang Yang ⋅ Xinrun Wang ⋅ Shuxin Li ⋅ Qinggang Zhang ⋅ Huachi Zhou ⋅ Zhuoyi Lin ⋅ Bo Li ⋅ Xiao Huang [Project Page](https://smu-diga.github.io/cslm/) [ [Poster](/media/PosterPDFs/NeurIPS%202026/140076.png?t=1794130458.009236 "Poster")]  [ [OpenReview](https://openreview.net/forum?id=OmubRAmSd7 "OpenReview")] ### Abstract The emergence of large language models (LMs) as versatile problem-solving systems marks a paradigm shift comparable to the advent of digital computers. Traditional computer science provides theoretical foundations for understanding computational processes through complexity theory, algorithms, and formal methods, this position paper argues that language models require their own distinct theoretical framework, termed as Computer Science of Language Models (**CSLM**). We identify seven fundamental differences between traditional computing and language model: 1) the generating-solving-verifying triad versus the solving-verifying dichotomy, 2) token-based rather than operation-based computation, 3) probabilistic reliability with hallucinations rather than deterministic correctness, 4) native multimodal understanding beyond pixel-level processing, 5) general-purpose capabilities versus problem-specific algorithms, 6) essential two-stage training-inference processes, and 7) inherent knowledge. We argue these differences necessitate new theoretical frameworks, complexity measures, and evaluation methodologies. Then, we define the **token complexity** as the core concept in CSLM and discuss connections to existing research in scaling laws, memory systems, tool use, and fine-tuning, while identifying critical open questions about LM-complete problems, reliability bounds, emergence phenomena, and multimodal complexity. Drawing parallels to complexity theory's 50-year development, we present a 5-year research roadmap (2026-2030) to build the mature CSLM. Traditional computer science provides theoretical foundations for understanding computational processes through complexity theory, algorithms, and formal methods, this position paper argues that language models require their own distinct theoretical framework, termed as Computer Science of Language Models (**CSLM**). We identify seven fundamental differences between traditional computing and language model: 1) the generating-solving-verifying triad versus the solving-verifying dichotomy, 2) token-based rather than operation-based computation, 3) probabilistic reliability with hallucinations rather than deterministic correctness, 4) native multimodal understanding beyond pixel-level processing, 5) general-purpose capabilities versus problem-specific algorithms, 6) essential two-stage training-inference processes, and 7) inherent knowledge. We argue these differences necessitate new theoretical frameworks, complexity measures, and evaluation methodologies. Then, we define the **token complexity** as the core concept in CSLM and discuss connections to existing research in scaling laws, memory systems, tool use, and fine-tuning, while identifying critical open questions about LM-complete problems, reliability bounds, emergence phenomena, and multimodal complexity. Drawing parallels to complexity theory's 50-year development, we present a 5-year research roadmap (2026-2030) to build the mature CSLM. LLMs.content: # How Large Language Models Work: A Plain-English Guide to AI Chatbots If you’ve spent any time typing prompts into ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini, you’ve probably experienced a moment of genuine wonder. You ask a complicated question, and within seconds, a blinking cursor outputs clean, articulate, and surprisingly insightful prose. It feels like there’s someone sitting on the other end thinking through your problem. **Spoiler: There isn’t.** Behind the conversational charm is a machine learning system known as a **Large Language Model (LLM)**. And while the engineering behind it is undeniably staggering, the fundamental principle is surprisingly simple. You don’t need a degree in linear algebra or computer science to understand how modern AI works. Here is the plain-English, no-nonsense breakdown of what LLMs are, how they learn, why they hallucinate, and how to get the most out of them. ## 1. The Core Idea: Autocomplete on Steroids Imagine you see the following incomplete sentence: > “The capital of France is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_.” Almost everyone reading this immediately thinks of **Paris**. You didn’t need to scan an encyclopedia or run a database query; your brain simply recognized a familiar linguistic pattern. At its core, **an LLM is trained to do this exact blank-filling task on an astronomical scale.** Instead of retrieving answers from a curated index of facts like Google Search does, a language model is an ultra-advanced prediction engine. It calculates what word (or fragment of a word) is statistically most likely to follow the text it has just seen. `Input: "The cat sat on the..." Model calculates probabilities: - "mat" (72%) - "floor" (15%) - "couch" (8%) - "moon" (0.01%)` By repeating this single micro-decision dozens of times per second — guessing one piece, appending it, and guessing the next — it produces cohesive paragraphs, generates working software code, translates languages, and reasons through complex ideas. ## 2. Tokens: How the Model Reads Text Computers don’t understand letters, words, or sentences the way humans do; they understand numbers. Before an LLM can process any text, it breaks words down into manageable fragments called **tokens**. > **Rule of thumb:** In English, 1 token is roughly equivalent to 0.75 words (or about 4 characters). 1,000 tokens translates to roughly 750 words. A token can represent: - An entire common word (e.g., `"apple"`) - Part of a word or syllable (e.g., `"un"`, `"pre"`, `"dictable"`) - Punctuation, spacing, or emojis (e.g., `!`, `?`, `🤖`) When AI companies talk about **context windows** (such as a 128k or 1-million token window), they are describing the maximum amount of text the model can hold in its active working memory at any single moment. ## 3. Parameters: Where the “Knowledge” Lives Inside every LLM are billions — sometimes hundreds of billions — of adjustable mathematical variables called **parameters** (or weights). Think of parameters as an immense mixing board with 70 billion dials in a sound recording studio: - During training, whenever the model makes an incorrect guess, the dials are nudged by a tiny fraction. - Over months of training across supercomputers, those dials settle into settings that reflect grammatical structures, historical facts, coding patterns, nuances, idioms, and conversational rhythm. > **Important Insight:** There is no single dial or folder marked “Abraham Lincoln” or “Quantum Mechanics.” Knowledge is distributed across millions of interconnected mathematical relationships. ## 4. AI Product.content: **As generative AI lowers the cost of creating new businesses, corporate investors are rethinking the relationship between external startups and internal venture building. The opportunity may lie in combining the two.** Generative AI is changing the economics of corporate innovation. As tools become more powerful and the cost of developing new products and services falls, companies have a growing incentive to build businesses themselves rather than invest in external startups. But that does not necessarily make corporate venture capital less relevant. Instead, it is prompting companies to rethink the relationship between investing in startups, building ventures internally and partnering with entrepreneurs. Discussions at Global Corporate Venturing events in New York, São Paulo, Tokyo, London, Singapore and San Francisco over the past six weeks suggest that the distinction between these activities is becoming increasingly blurred. One recurring theme, raised by attendees at the GCV Executive Leadership Forum in New York, was that successful innovation still depends on entrepreneurial talent and founder-led ideas, whether those founders are working inside or outside a corporation. The question for corporate venturers is increasingly what a company can contribute to a new business that an independent startup would struggle to access. That might be proprietary data, customer relationships, technical expertise, distribution or the ability to operate at scale. This is also a theme emerging from GCV’s annual venture builder survey: the corporate advantage should be more than simply providing capital or a parent company’s name. In Singapore, discussions pointed to growing interest among local corporates in moving beyond passive investment towards co-venture building. Government-backed launchpad initiatives are helping to encourage this approach, with companies looking at opportunities to create new businesses rather than simply take stakes in existing ones. The two models can also work together, as the experience of Brazilian bank Itaú Unibanco and generative AI startup NeoSpace AI illustrates. Itaú’s corporate venture capital unit, led by Philippe Schlumpf, previously led an $18m funding round in NeoSpace in early 2025, taking a 15% stake. The bank has since agreed to acquire the startup for R$2.925bn ($589m). Under the proposed arrangement, NeoSpace will bring its dedicated AI research team into the bank while continuing to operate independently under its existing chief executive, Bruno Pierobon. The deal illustrates how corporate investment can provide a route to a deeper strategic relationship. An initial minority stake gives a company exposure to an emerging technology and its entrepreneurial team; a subsequent acquisition can bring those capabilities closer to the core business. For the startup, the relationship offers access to a major corporate customer and the resources to develop its technology. For the corporate investor, it provides a way to identify and build relationships with talent and capabilities that might be difficult to develop internally. Yet access to technology and entrepreneurial talent is only part of the challenge. Companies also need to create internal environments in which innovation can flourish. Harvard Business School professor Linda Hill’s research highlights the importance of involving employees in innovation, rather than treating it as the responsibility of a specialist team. Her recommendations include recognising innovation as anything new and useful to an organisation, building teams around individual strengths, connecting everyday work to a wider purpose and explaining not just the rules but the reasons behind them. AI Product.content: Meanwhile, businesses are rapidly adopting generative AI tools to improve efficiency, automate routine tasks, and assist with decision-making, including the use of large language models (ie, LLMs), which understand, predict, and generate human language. Employees from organizations across industries may be using generative AI in the office for administrative tasks like summarizing emails, drafting documents, analyzing spreadsheets, and more. In some cases, these uses entail business owners and their employees inputting confidential business, customer, or employee information into these systems. That use spans both public AI tools (consumer-facing services on the open internet such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Google Gemini) and enterprise AI tools (company-controlled systems configured to preserve confidentiality and compliance). This rapid adoption and explosion of novel use cases is creating legal, regulatory, and ethical risks that have not yet been fully addressed under existing legal frameworks. Courts are being confronted with first-impression issues across evolving fact patterns, and their decisions will affect businesses of all sizes. Generative AI use in the workplace spans across a variety of firms, agencies, and companies. For instance, financial advisors may be entering client financial goals, account balances and holdings into these tools. Insurance adjusters may be drafting claim summaries and customer correspondence based on accident reports, photographs, medical records, and policy information. Real estate agents may be drafting purchase agreements, summarizing inspection reports, and preparing client communications. Engineering firm employees may be reviewing technical specifications and drafting project reports based on propriety designs, and client requirements. Software developers may be generating code or debugging applications by inputting proprietary source code and internal documentation. In addition, employees from organizations across industries may be using generative AI in the office for administrative tasks like summarizing emails, drafting documents, analyzing spreadsheets, and more. One of the most significant legal risks businesses face when using generative AI is the potential loss of trade secret protection. Marketing-specific guardrails can keep off-brand content from going public. ### Share this article ### Table of Contents ### Table of Contents ### Spy on Any Website Enterprise AI governance addresses security, privacy, and compliance risks, but it often overlooks brand consistency. As AI gives employees across the organization the power to create content, marketing must help establish guardrails that protect brand identity without stifling creativity. I’ve spent the last few months speaking with creative and marketing leaders across the country about how AI is changing their roles. One concern keeps coming up: the loss of brand control as more employees create content without marketing oversight. One story I heard illustrates the risk. Late one evening, an enthusiastic CEO decided to publish a thought leadership piece without involving the creative team. They opened a generative AI tool, typed a quick prompt, and published an AI-generated image directly to the company’s external channels. The result was painfully off-brand. The visuals had that recognizable synthetic gloss and strange AI artifacts. The messaging lacked the brand’s usual warmth and contradicted the voice the company spent years cultivating. Trying to apply a single blanket policy just drives people to unapproved shadow tools. AI Product.content: One of generative AI’s biggest promises is the idea that it can help smaller companies and startups take on established firms by providing access to advanced capabilities. Yet since the introduction of ChatGPT in 2022, investors have placed their biggest bets on the more dominant companies—those they saw as best positioned to benefit from the new technology, according to research by Harvard Business School Professor Suraj Srinivasan. And they were rewarded: these companies’ returns outperformed their peers’ by 19 percentage points in the year following the platform’s launch. ChatGPT sparked the imaginations of leaders at companies of every size and industry when it emerged four years ago, with investors watching closely. So far, large organizations have made more progress on adopting AI agents than smaller firms, according to a McKinsey survey. Srinivasan’s findings—detailed in the working paper “Generative AI and Market Expectations of Superstar Firms”—shed light on why. While “lean organizations might adopt the new technologies faster; complex ones have more friction to remove, and thus greater benefits from adopting these technologies,” says Srinivasan, the Philip J. Stomberg Professor of Business Administration. Srinivasan coauthored the paper, updated in September, with Wilbur Chen, a professor at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, and Bullipe R. Chintha, a professor at the Singapore Institute of Technology. ## Does innovation topple leaders—or strengthen them? The researchers set out to test a question raised by French economist Philippe Aghion in his 2025 Nobel Prize lecture: does a major technological shift topple dominant firms—or lock them in? The answer they arrived at—that the market favors complex organizations already doing work AI is best at—surprised Srinivasan and his colleagues. “In hindsight, the economics make sense,” he says. “A large superstar firm is, among other things, an expensive machine for moving information.” But the premium wasn't just about organizational complexity. The study found that these companies also gained from their research and operational know-how, and deep benches of data talent. The gen AI premium ran 28 and 29 points, among firms rich in these two categories of intangible assets, respectively, and was absent among firms without them. ## What sets superstar AI companies apart To answer Aghion’s question, Srinivasan and his team analyzed 2,596 US companies, leveraging data from Compustat and the Center for Research in Security Prices. The researchers were particularly interested in “superstars,” which they defined as the top 10% of companies by market value relative to their invested tangible and intangible capital. They calculated that relationship using an adjusted version of Tobin's Q, a widely used valuation measure. To identify firms that are more likely to be affected by generative AI, the team used occupational data from Revelio Labs to measure their workforce exposure to the technology. Firms scoring above the sample’s median were classified as “highly exposed” to the technology. After mapping the companies across those dimensions, “we then tracked their returns in the months following ChatGPT’s release as a measure of investors’ revised expectations about their future performance,” Srinivasan says. The researchers were surprised to see “how sharply the market separated the GenAI-aligned superstars from others,” Srinivasan says. At the two-year mark, the study found that the market’s conviction in its judgment only got stronger: the higher return of superstar firms highly engaged with AI’s best side had doubled to 39 points from the first-year premium. ## Do superstars always win? Srinivasan and his team considered other potential explanations for why investors may have favored highly AI-exposed superstar companies over their peers. [Nvidia](/tag/nvidia) reported data center revenue of $107.6 billion, an increase of 110 per cent from the previous year. The company disclosed [financial guarantees](/tag/financial+guarantees) of up to $118 billion tied to [AI infrastructure](/tag/ai+infrastructure) projects. These guarantees are designed to help customers finance and build [facilities](/tag/facilities) with sufficient [power](/tag/power) for large AI workloads. The largest guarantee, valued at up to $105 billion, supports [SB Energy](/tag/sb+energy)’s PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in [Ohio](/tag/ohio). This campus will host Nvidia infrastructure under 20-year leases to [OpenAI](/tag/openai), covering approximately 4.25 GW across nine buildings. Nvidia’s guarantee exposure for PORTS-Pike will build as buildings come online, with the first expected in fiscal 2029. The exposure will decline over the lease terms as OpenAI makes payments. The $118 billion maximum gross exposure also includes $9.5 billion in power and systems credit support guarantees. Additionally, $3.5 billion is allocated for land, power, and shell guarantees for neocloud providers. Separately, Nvidia reported $32 billion in future commitments under neocloud agreements. These commitments are contingent on providers securing their own financing, purchasing Nvidia infrastructure, and deploying the computing capacity. Stephen Sopko, practice lead for semiconductor and deep tech at HyperFrame Research, noted that $105 billion of the guarantees backs the PORTS-Pike campus, leased to OpenAI for 20 years. The company also expanded packaging at Siliconware Precision Industries (SPIL) and Amkor Technology. Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Google Cloud announced the general availability of Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs. Infra & Chips.content: Nvidia reported $107.6 billion in data center revenue Tuesday, up 110% from a year earlier, and disclosed up to $118 billion in financial guarantees tied to AI infrastructure projects. The guarantees put Nvidia on the hook for financing arrangements designed to help customers secure the land, power and facilities needed to deploy its systems. The impressive quarter comes on the heels of a startling scandal that led to CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster and dominated headlines around the world. Huang resigned Nov. 12 after reports of multiple affairs, including one with a woman suspected by U.S. intelligence officials of having ties to Chinese intelligence. CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO while the board seeks a permanent successor. The campaign to bring Huang back attracted prominent supporters, including Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and President Donald Trump. A public petition drew more than 180,000 signatures, including thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees. Huang said Tuesday he would be honored to return if the board decided it was in the company’s best interests. The board rejected that possibility during Tuesday’s earnings call. Chairman Harvey Jones said directors unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation and did not intend to reinstate him. The board will consider internal and external candidates for a permanent CEO. The leadership upheaval comes as Nvidia takes on a larger role in financing and securing the infrastructure needed to sustain its AI growth. For data center operators, Nvidia’s guarantees address a constraint that comes before server deployment: financing and building facilities with enough power to support large AI workloads. Nvidia is helping customers bridge that gap while securing the components needed to manufacture its next generations of systems. The largest guarantee supports SB Energy’s PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Ohio. Nvidia is providing credit support for approximately 4.25 gigawatts across nine buildings. The campus will host Nvidia infrastructure under 20-year leases to OpenAI, subject to limited exceptions. As buildings come online, Nvidia’s guarantee exposure will build. Each guarantee takes effect only after its associated building is completed and ready for service. The first is expected in fiscal 2029. Exposure will reach a maximum of $105 billion and then decline over the lease terms as OpenAI makes payments. Nvidia said it had made no guarantee payments as of Oct. 25. Infra & Chips.title: Nvidia's AI Financing Guarantees Hit $118 Billion. Kress Clarifies When They Take Effect.
Infra & Chips.titleZh: Nvidia's AI Financing Guarantees Hit $118 Billion. Kress Clarifies When They Take Effect.
Infra & Chips.content: Nvidia's financial guarantees tied to artificial intelligence infrastructure have climbed to $118 billion, up $9.5 billion from the previous quarter, as interim CEO Colette Kress clarified when the chipmaker could become liable for payments involving its data center partners. The figure represents Nvidia's maximum potential exposure under various financing arrangements, rather than money already spent or an immediate obligation to pay. According to the company's latest financial commentary filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the guarantees would require Nvidia to make payments to third parties only if certain partners default on their obligations and the applicable conditions are met. The total has increased from $108.5 billion disclosed in the previous quarter, primarily reflecting an additional $9.5 billion in power and systems credit support guarantees. Nvidia said it has not made any payments under its guarantees. The largest exposure comes from a $105 billion arrangement supporting SB Energy's PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Ohio, a major AI infrastructure project that will host Nvidia computing systems under long-term leases to OpenAI. The arrangement, originally disclosed in August, covers approximately 4.25 gigawatts of capacity across nine data center buildings. Each guarantee becomes effective only after its corresponding building is completed and ready for service. Nvidia expects the first building to meet those conditions in fiscal 2029, with its potential exposure increasing in stages as additional facilities become operational. The guarantees are structured to decline over the 20-year lease terms as OpenAI makes payments. The remaining $13 billion consists of $3.5 billion in guarantees supporting land, power and building infrastructure for other AI cloud operators, along with $9.5 billion in power and systems credit support. Kress addressed the financing arrangements during Tuesday's earnings conference call, responding to questions about whether Nvidia was changing how it supports specialized AI cloud providers, commonly known as neoclouds. Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon questioned language in Nvidia's latest financial disclosures stating that certain commitments would take effect only after the operators secured financing to purchase computing infrastructure and brought the relevant capacity into operation. Kress explained that companies must first arrange the necessary debt or equity financing, complete construction and prepare the computing infrastructure for use before the relevant guarantees become effective.
